@@114559496 <h> Bold Targets and Breakthroughs for India 's Climate Resilience <h> The effects of climate change on public health in India can no longer be ignored . <p> Are we prepared for the climate crisis staring us in the face ? The Quint wants to go big on telling the most important stories of our time . Support us to tell them . Become a member now . <p> In India , the effects of climate change are far-reaching and complex , from the erratic pattern of rains and its impact on agriculture to the rise in sea levels affecting the cities along the coasts . The Indian political system , the academic community and various stakeholders are in the pursuit of new ideas , setting concrete measures to boost climate resilience . <p> A particular sector of interest is agriculture , as it is a sensitive sector of the economy of India and is most affected by a changing climate . It supports the livelihoods of millions of people . Climate-smart agriculture practices like the introduction of drought-resistant varieties of crops or technological advancement through drones and precision farming are , however , big steps . Simultaneously , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of climate alternate shelters are included in the ambitious , hard measures to fight climate change . <p> India 's commitment to international agreements underscores its dedication to global cooperation in addressing climate impacts . By fostering collaborations on both national and international levels , India aims to build resilient systems that protect vulnerable populations and ensure sustainable development for future generations . <p> Dr Nisha Mendiratta , Executive Director of Indo-U.S . Science and Technology Forum ( IUSSTF ) , emphasises , " Climate change is a global phenomenon that poses a significant threat to human health . " The increasing frequency and intensity of extreme weather events lead to rising mortality rates , the spread of diseases , and heightened vulnerabilities among marginalised communities . Addressing these challenges requires a coordinated , multi-pronged , and globally integrated response . <h> The Challenges of Climate-Induced Health Issues <p> The effects of climate change on public health in India can no longer be ignored , as high temperatures , erratic weather conditions , and natural calamities like floods and heat waves are adversely affecting people 's health . These changes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the transmission of vector-borne diseases such as dengue and malaria , and cause complications in the respiratory system as air pollution increases . <p> Vulnerable groups , especially those living in low-income locations in urban areas and people in rural and coastal zones , are more at risk . This is because they are devoid of basic infrastructure to survive , which has a direct impact on health and nutrition . To meet these challenges , it is necessary to develop integrated public health policies and devise strategies that would help develop resilience in populations against climate change and its various impacts . <p> Understanding the full impact of climate change necessitates recognising its direct and indirect effects on health . Dr Purvi Patel , a climate change and health expert , explains , " Climate change impacts health directly through extreme weather events and indirectly through high pollution , sea level rise , elevated temperatures , and extreme precipitation . " These factors collectively result in an increased burden of both communicable and non-communicable diseases , posing a dual challenge for the health sector . <p> While international efforts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ vital role . India 's National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health ( NPCCHH ) is an illustrative example . Dr Patel explains , " NPCCHH is strengthening the healthcare system through extensive training programs , " highlighting its efforts to prepare health systems for climate-sensitive diseases . <p> Effective public health strategies should integrate various facets such as meteorology , disaster risk reduction , air and water quality , and energy efficiency . Dr Patel emphasises the importance of " sensitising various stakeholders and communities to the health impacts of climate change and advocating for health-centred climate responses . " <h> The Role of International Partnerships <p> Resilient societies can be built and sustained through international partnerships , as there is an exchange of knowledge , resources and strategies . These collaborations allow countries to implement the resilience models and technological advances that have worked for others , thus improving the capacities to deal with climate change . <p> For example , the various international agreements promote cohesion and exchange of technology , which is necessary in finding solutions to persistent issues . <p> International partnerships also support @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ areas and populations at risk of discrimination , inequality , and less favourable policies by integrating knowledge , manpower and funds . Such collaboration enhances response to dangers that are posed on a global level ; hence , the outcome is a better society and the world . <h> Social Equity and Climate Adaptation <p> Achieving climate resilience requires a strong focus on social equity . Dr Ananya Chakraborti , Senior Research Specialist in climate Resilience Practice at the World Resources Institute ( WRI ) , India , stresses , " Resilience measures in the Indian farm sector must consider the impacts of such measures on women and marginalised social groups . " Climate adaptation strategies that overlook these groups risk increasing labour burdens and reducing adoption rates of interventions like climate-resilient seeds . <p> Effective climate resilience initiatives must consider the impacts on women and marginalised groups . Programs that involve local communities and cater to specific needs are more likely to succeed and promote equitable adaptation measures . <p> Advanced technologies and innovative interventions , such as using drones in agriculture or developing climate-resilient infrastructures , can greatly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ core consideration to ensure these measures ' long-term viability . <p> The pressing implications of climate change require urgent and collaborative action across all governance levels and sectors . Voices like Dr Mendiratta 's and Dr Chakraborti 's remind us that we can secure a healthier and more sustainable future for all through collective endeavours focusing on equity , sustainability , and resilience . <p> Dr Mendiratta said , " Let 's take bold action now for a healthier and more sustainable future . " By leveraging the power of international partnerships and diverse strategies , the global community can effectively tackle the health impacts of climate change and pave the way towards resilience and equity . <h> Embracing Global Partnerships and Innovation <p> In the face of escalating climate threats , India recognises the imperative for bold targets and groundbreaking interventions to achieve climate resilience . As one of the most climate-vulnerable nations , India experiences severe weather impacts , affecting millions dependent on agriculture and causing public health crises . Tackling these challenges necessitates coordinated efforts at both national and international levels . @@114559608 <p> Saffron has long been more than just a crop for the people of Kashmir valley , it is a symbol of heritage and a vital source of income for local farmers . But its farming is facing significant sustainability and livelihood issues , highlighting the urgent need for suitable technologies to combat global warming . <p> As global temperatures rise , the very foundations of this traditional cultivation industry are under siege . Erratic weather patterns , unseasonable warmth , and diminishing snowfall have disrupted the delicate balance required for saffron cultivation . <p> Saffron production , which once reached nearly 17 tons annually , has now declined and stabilised at around 15 tons per year . <p> Farmers who have invested their lives in saffron farming are now facing uncertainty and declining yields , jeopardizing their livelihoods . <p> However , the technology and research being developed by the Advanced Research Centre for Saffron and Seed Spices in the Pampore district of Jammu and Kashmir -- the only Saffron research centre in India -- is continuously engaged in increasing the production of the crop . <p> " Due to changing weather patterns , the research centre has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , detailing when and how much irrigation the crop requires , has been shared with the Department of Agriculture . <p> The research centre has provided comprehensive guidance covering all aspects of saffron cultivation , from land preparation and seed sowing to intercultural operations , harvesting , and post-harvest management , which is now accessible to our farmers , " Bashir Ahmad Ilahi , Professor in Head Saffron Research Station , Pampore , told ANI . <p> He said that saffron seeds are ideally sown in late July , with the crucial condition that the soil remains moist but not waterlogged . <p> " The flowers typically begin to bloom between October 10 and 15 , and harvesting occurs regularly by November 15 . India 's solar revolution set an initial goal of generating 20 GW of solar power by 2022 . By ramping @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Government resources that would otherwise be spent on subsidising fossil fuels , allowing more investment in infrastructure , healthcare , and education . By shifting toward solar energy , India can significantly reduce its carbon footprint and contribute to the global fight against climate change . The large-scale deployment of solar power could help India meet its international climate commitments to achieve net-zero emissions by 2070 and generate 50 percent of its energy from renewable sources by 2030 . Solarisation also has profound social implications , particularly for rural and underserved communities . Millions of people in India still lack access to reliable electricity , and many more experience frequent blackouts . Historically , the Indian rhinoceros once roamed across a vast range that extended from the foothills of the Himalayas in northern India and Nepal to northeastern India and the plains of Bhutan . <p> By the mid-20th century , the rhino population became severely fragmented , confined to the swampy grasslands of Assam and parts of Nepal . Deforestation and the conversion of these fertile lands into agricultural areas pushed the species to the brink . Poaching for the horn , which has immense value in traditional medicine , particularly in China and Southeast Asia , further aggravated the situation . <p> Early Conservation Efforts <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , including vast economic development and rebuilding the nation . Wildlife conservation was not a top priority in these formative years . However , by the 1950s and 1960s , conservationists began to realise the perilous situation of India 's wildlife , including the rhino . The sprawling Kaziranga National Park became a focal point of these early efforts for its rich biodiversity . <p> Rhinos are often solitary and their shy behaviour makes it hard to track them consistently , leading to doubtful population counts <p> Kaziranga was established as a reserve forest in 1905 by Mary Curzon , the wife of then Viceroy of India , Lord Curzon , but it was n't until 1950 that it officially gained the status of a wildlife sanctuary and graduated to National Park . The protection offered by this sanctuary was limited in scope at the time , with few resources allocated for wildlife protection , but it was a beginning . Throughout the 1960s and 1970s , as awareness of conservation issues grew globally , India 's commitment to preserving the rhino strengthened . <p> Landmark in Conservation <p> In @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the rhinoceros , a symbol of regional pride . Though Kaziranga was a sanctuary for rhinos , increased poaching and habitat threats led to conservation concerns . Their population had already dwindled , and by 1983 , poaching had claimed over 90 rhinos . This situation distressed former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi , who , despite local opposition , supported a translocation effort to protect the species . A strong decision to translocate rhinos from Assam to the Dudhwa National Park in Uttar Pradesh took concrete shape . Dudhwa grasslands resembled Assam 's , making it an ideal location . In 1984 , five rhinos were airlifted in a specially commissioned Russian cargo plane , accompanied by environmentalists . <p> Many in Assam feared that relocating rhinos would diminish their cultural significance and weaken the State 's claim to the species . Despite these objections , Indira Gandhi 's support played a pivotal role in this historic conservation effort , ensuring the rhinos ' survival beyond Assam while fostering a national approach to protecting endangered species . It was found to be between 130,000 and 100,000 years old . <p> The second fossil , a skull , belonged a juvenile polar bear and was found the Beaufort Sea near Alaska . @@114563597 <h> Book Excerpt : Shashi Tharoor on the environment and words <p> Environmental consciousness has been on the increase globally , and inevitably has infiltrated our language as well with new terms to give us a vocabulary to cope with new ecological challenges . <p> It 's only in the last couple of decades that we have come to realize that we are all living in the Anthropocene , defined as a geological epoch marked by significant human impact on Earth 's geology and ecosystems , including climate change . Terms like ' ecology ' , ' biodiversity ' , and ' greenhouse gas emissions ' are , of course , better known and have been widely in use for a bit longer , but even they were largely unheard of before the 1960s . <p> Some of the basic environmental vocabulary we all need to have would feature these terms : <p> * Pollution : the introduction of contaminants into the natural environment that cause adverse change . <p> * Ecosystem : all the plants and animals in a particular area , together with their surrounding environment . The destruction of habitat in a particular area can be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ deterioration of the environment through the depletion of resources such as air , water , and soil and the extinction of wildlife . <p> * Resource depletion : the consumption of natural resources faster than they can be replenished . <p> * Biodiversity loss : The reduction in the variety and variability of life forms on Earth . <p> But we have moved beyond the basics to more exotic terms than these . As far back as the 1940s , the author J. R. R. Tolkien , creator of the famous The Lord of the Rings , invented the term ' eucatastrophe ' , which he suggested was a ' good ' catastrophe . Environmentalists know all about bad catastrophes that can threaten the very survival of the human race -- supervolcanoes , nuclear winter , uncontrolled global warming , pandemics , a meteor colliding with the Earth . But what about those environmental disasters that led to a happy development ? For example , some environmental catastrophe hundreds of millions of years ago wiped out dinosaurs from the earth . But their extinction led to the survival of mammals @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an eucatastrophe . <p> An intriguing pair , Heidi Quante and Alicia Escott , artists who specialize in environmental vocabulary , have spent a decade collecting and creating new words on the environment in the name of what they call the Bureau of Linguistical Reality . But their neologisms are a bit too exotic to catch on easily -- terms like ' nonnapaura ' ( derived from Italian , to describe the combination of hope and fear many feel for the future because of the global environmental crisis ) , ' chucosol ' ( of El Salvadorian and Korean origin , to describe the ' dirty sun ' effect of sunsets viewed through polluted air ) or ' shellaqua ' ( derived from ' shellac ' and ' aqua ' , or water , for the act of covering a once-permeable surface like sand with human-made materials like tar or macadam , increasing the risk of floods ) . For instance , they have combined pre + euphoria + eau ( the French word for water ) to come up with ' preuphoreau ' , for the bodily feeling of sensing a change in the atmosphere because rain is coming . ( Again , it can also describe a moment of hopeful anticipation of imminent change ) . It 's clever , no doubt , but can most people pronounce it ? <p> In the ' not-yet-popular ' category of neologisms the pair have also coined terms like ' sandulate ' , a verb which means to understand that the coastline is alive , so we ca n't just build solid structures on it but must respect it . The attitude of some people that if the world is destroyed by environmental catastrophe , Mars could one day offer Earthlings a refuge from climate change , is termed ' marsification ' . <p> Even if these terms remain obscure , arguably , the phenomenon @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ back as 1909 , changes in our environment gave English a new word : in reaction to widespread air pollution , a word was coined that combined smoke and fog into ' smog ' . So there 's nothing new under the sun , except where ( as in Delhi 's National Capital Region ) the pollution is so bad that you ca n't see it

The approach is both pragmatic and putting India 's interest first . <h> INDIA 'S BALANCING ACT <p> India 's foreign policy doctrine of ' strategic autonomy ' has long been a cornerstone of its international relations . This approach , rooted in the nation 's post-colonial experience and its commitment to non-alignment during the Cold War , prioritises independent decision-making in foreign affairs , avoiding entanglement in great power rivalries and preserving the ability to forge partnerships based on national interest rather than ideological alignment . This has allowed India to cultivate robust relationships with a diverse array of nations . <p> A prime example of this delicate balancing act is India 's relationship with both Russia and the West , particularly the United States . The US , in particular , has emerged as a key partner for India , with growing cooperation in areas such as defence , trade and technology . Recently , both the countries signed the Security of Supplies Arrangement which will streamline the process for both countries to acquire critical defence equipment from each other , ensuring a reliable supply chain even during unforeseen crises . <p> The ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict has placed significant strain on India 's ability to maintain this delicate balance . Western powers , led by the United States , have imposed stringent sanctions on Russia and have actively sought to isolate it diplomatically . <p> India 's response to the conflict has been characterised by a nuanced and pragmatic approach . It has refrained from explicitly condemning Russia 's actions , abstaining from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with Moscow , including the purchase of discounted Russian oil . This stance has drawn criticism from some Western quarters , who have urged India to take a more forceful stand against Russia . However , India has defended its position , arguing that it is acting in its own national interest and that dialogue and diplomacy are the only path to a peaceful resolution of the conflict . <p> India 's approach reflects a broader shift in the global landscape towards multipolarity . The rise of China , coupled with the resurgence of Russia , has challenged USA 's unipolarity that characterised the post-Cold War era . @@114623287 <h> How Shortcuts Across the Skies Can Make Flights Greener : Q&amp;A <h> Getting from A to B faster is generally the goal of most travelers , particularly for those flying long-haul in economy . <p> Bloomberg <p> Published23 Sep 2024 , 03:01 AM IST <p> How Shortcuts Across the Skies Can Make Flights Greener : Q&amp;A <p> ( Bloomberg ) -- Getting from A to B faster is generally the goal of most travelers , particularly for those flying long-haul in economy . <p> Now , under a trial that started last month in Asia , shaving precious minutes off hours-long trips is a reality , depending upon what route a pilot chooses to take across the skies . <p> Since early August , air crew on selected routes between Singapore , Jakarta and a handful of cities in Australia and New Zealand have had the flexibility to choose the most direct and efficient path to get there . It 's about saving time , but also fuel , hence limiting greenhouse gas emissions . <p> Deviating from the fixed network of invisible highways that etch planes ' trajectories around the world and instead allowing a unique flight @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's not as dangerous as it sounds . <p> Here 's a look at how it works . <p> 1 . What is the trial ? <p> Singapore , Australia , Indonesia and New Zealand have banded together to make better use of their airspace to trial quicker , more direct flight paths . <p> The three-month trial started Aug. 5 and will be reviewed in November with a possible view to expanding it to more cities and airlines . <p> The carriers involved are Singapore Airlines Ltd. , Qantas Airways Ltd. , Air New Zealand Ltd. and Garuda Indonesia and they 're able to take shortcuts on 38 routes using what 's called user-preferred routing ( UPR ) . <p> Singapore Airlines has said that it 's using the trial on 15 routes , including to Sydney , Christchurch , Darwin and Perth . Garuda said it 's operating user-preferred routing on flights from Jakarta to Sydney and Melbourne . <p> Other destinations involved include Brisbane , Cairns and Adelaide . <p> 2 . What 's behind the trial ? <p> In short , climate change . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the thinking is that over time , fuel and carbon emissions savings will multiply . <p> The Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore , in a statement Aug. 15 , said that airlines can potentially save up to 1,700 kilograms of fuel for a flight between Singapore and Melbourne and more than 1,960 tonnes of carbon emissions a year for that route over a year of daily flights . <p> With about 10 flights a day each way , or some 7,745 scheduled flights between the two cities this year , according to data from Cirium , the numbers should start to add up . <p> But user-preferred routing is n't a silver bullet , especially considering the volume of flights is also rising , particularly in Asia , home to some of the fastest-growing air travel markets . <p> McKinsey &amp; Co. has estimated some $5 trillion of capital investment may be needed to deliver on aviation 's goal of reaching carbon neutrality by 2050 , almost all of it plowed into sustainable fuel production and renewable power generation . <p> Making flights 10 to 15 minutes shorter generally does @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ airspace trials happened before ? <p> User-preferred routing has been trialled as far back as 2008 and in some places , like Australia , a vast continent that has its own say over its airspace , it 's already happening . <p> Internationally , the practice has been limited due to the complexity of coordinating routes across national boundaries . Airservices Australia says it gets tricky when airspace is managed by different air navigation operators . <p> In New Zealand , another place that 's relatively geographically isolated , around 65% of flights across its some 26 million square kilometers of airspace use shortcuts where possible . <p> 4 . How do pilots arrange shortcuts and what role do air traffic controllers play ? <p> Pilots typically follow waypoints , or fixed points in the sky to help planes navigate safely . <p> Under user-preferred routing , pilots and their operations teams manually plug the most efficient route as they see it into flight planning software , taking into account things like wind speed and direction , turbulence and other environmental and weather factors . The flight planning system then @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ says that " pilots and controllers are encouraged not to amend routes without good reason as most user-preferred routes are n't the shortest distance in track miles . " The aim is to spend " the shortest time in the air , therefore flying a straight line between departure and arrival points is often not the most efficient route . " <p> Airways , New Zealand 's air navigation service provider , says it 's then up to air traffic controllers to " facilitate " these shortcut routes taking into account what other flights are happening at the same time . <p> 5 . It sounds potentially dangerous . Is it safe ? <p> Completely . Airlines and aviation regulators are in no doubt about the benefits and the operational safety behind user-preferred routing . <p> All trips are signed off on by air traffic controllers , whose job is to help safely navigate and manage airspace . There 's absolutely no freewheeling by pilots across the sky mid-flight , unless guided and advised by air traffic control staff on the ground . <p> " We do not share multiple @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ once after the final flight plan has been set , " Garuda President Irfan Setiaputra said in a statement . <p> 6 . How 's the trial in Asia going so far ? <p> Airservices Australia says there 's been anecdotal evidence of " considerable savings " for airlines in terms of fuel and carbon emissions , although declined to elaborate . <p> " Some flights have better results than others , " it said . " The variability in conditions means that every flight is different . " <p> Garuda said the trial has allowed the carrier to " utilize tail wind conditions to make flight operations faster as well as more fuel efficient . " <p> Other participating airlines declined to offer specific data while the trail is underway . <p> 7 . Are there plans for trials beyond Asia ? <p> Europe has sought to do something similar for 20 years under the Single European Sky initiative . <p> Aviation bodies and airlines from the continent have long tried to reform the congested airspace and effectively integrate the skies above almost 30 countries . <p> Under the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ achieved , by 2020 , an improvement in safety performance by a factor of 10 , a 10% reduction in the impact flights have on the environment , a reduction in the cost of air-traffic management services to airspace users by at least 50% and a three-fold increase in capacity where needed . <p> It has n't worked out that way , with countries opting to hang onto their national air navigation service providers , and therefore benefits , like making the continent 's airspace cheaper , yet to be realized . <p> In the US , user-preferred routing is also new , with United Airlines Holdings Inc. completing its first such flight only in mid-2020 , over Russia . In May 2023 , the Federal Aviation Administration activated 169 new , set routes along the US east coast that are more direct , saving passengers time , and airlines fuel .

Marshall saw the copper hoard objects as belonging to an age of bronze which , he believed , could be correlated with what was then termed the Early Vedic Age . @@114623317 <h> All eyes were on UPSC 's Ethics paper in a year when ethical issues around Puja Khedkar row and the lateral entry debate kept the institution in the headlines . Meanwhile UPSC upgraded the quality of its questions by challenging candidates to see many contemporary issues from the prism of ethics . Here 's our analysis . <p> UPSC Civil Services Mains Exam 's Ethics paper was n't a usual paper like the past year . Questions in section A challenged candidates to apply ethics to contemporary issues and prove that this exam is n't about ethical knowledge but ethical competency . The length of the paper tested the examinees ' performance and smart approach to questions . <p> UPSC conducted General Studies Paper 4 , as part of the Civil Services Main Exam 2024 on September 22 . There were 12 questions divided into two sections -- A ( theory ) and B ( case studies ) . Total marks were 250 marks and the time duration was three hours . Here 's what the paper asked : <h> Section A ( Theory ) - 150 words , 10 marks each <p> 1 . The buzzword ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( a ) . In fact , asking specific questions from popular themes was the tone of the paper throughout . While not all aspirants would have hit the bull 's eye , surely a smart candidate would have replaced the general points with desired terms to make it look like a tailor-fit answer . Yet this traditional knowledge , passed through word-of-mouth down the generations , has not remained limited to simply being a medium of connectivity , but is also a source of livelihood through tourism , and an inspiration for a new form of architecture . <p> Traditionally , the making of a root bridge first involves planting a Ficus sapling on the banks of a river , on one or both sides . Once it reaches maturity , the tree 's aerial roots are guided to the other side of the river through the hollowed-out trunk of a betel nut tree , with the support of a bamboo framework . <p> When the roots reach the other end , they are planted in the soil . @@114624903 <h> India in QUAD <p> India , a key player in the Quad alliance , made significant commitments that will not only benefit the region but also showcase its leadership in global diplomacy . Here 's a breakdown of the major initiatives and India 's role in driving them forward . <h> Quad Cancer Moonshot : A Lifesaving Health Initiative <p> One of the most significant outcomes of the Quad Summit was the launch of the " Quad Cancer Moonshot , " a comprehensive effort to improve cancer care across the Indo-Pacific . India 's contribution is pivotal in this initiative . The country has committed US$7.5 million worth of HPV sampling kits , detection tools , and cervical cancer vaccines to Indo-Pacific nations . Furthermore , India 's Serum Institute , in partnership with Gavi , will support orders of up to 40 million HPV vaccine doses . This collaboration is a major step forward in combating preventable cancers in the region , with India at the forefront of the health campaign . <p> Moreover , India will also provide $10 million to the WHO 's Global Initiative on Digital Health , offering technical assistance and capacity building @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( DPI ) . This combination of financial aid , vaccines , and digital infrastructure reflects the Quad 's commitment to saving lives and improving healthcare across the Indo-Pacific . <h> Strengthening Maritime Security : Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission <p> The Quad nations announced the first-ever " Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission " to take place in 2025 . This mission aims to improve the interoperability of Coast Guards across the Indo-Pacific while advancing maritime safety . India , with its extensive coastline and strategic location , will play a crucial role in ensuring that the region 's waters are more secure and free from illegal activities . <p> This initiative aligns with other maritime efforts like the " Maritime Initiative for Training in the Indo-Pacific " ( MAITRI ) , which India will spearhead by hosting its inaugural workshop during its Quad Presidency in 2025 . Through MAITRI , Indo-Pacific partners will be trained to better monitor and secure their waters , enhancing maritime governance across the region . <p> The " Quad Ports of the Future Partnership " is another major initiative designed to develop sustainable and resilient port @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ports remain operational during disruptions such as pandemics , natural disasters , and cyber or terrorist attacks . India will host the inaugural Quad Ports of the Future Partnership conference , bringing together the expertise of Quad members to promote best practices in maintaining port infrastructure . <p> As part of its broader infrastructure development strategy , India also committed to hosting a capacity-building workshop with the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure ( CDRI ) . This initiative focuses on enhancing the resilience of infrastructure against the backdrop of growing climate challenges in the region . <h> Boosting Semiconductor Supply Chains : A Contingency Network for the Future <p> The Quad also recognized the importance of diversifying and securing semiconductor supply chains , a critical aspect of global technology infrastructure . The four nations agreed to establish a " Semiconductor Supply Chains Contingency Network , " aiming to leverage the strengths of each member to create a more competitive and resilient market . This cooperation will enhance the Quad 's capacity to respond to disruptions in semiconductor supplies , which have become increasingly vital in both economic and security contexts @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ efficiency is another area where the Quad is aiming to make strides , particularly through the deployment of high-efficiency , affordable cooling systems across the Indo-Pacific . This initiative is part of a collective effort to address energy needs and mitigate the impacts of climate change . <p> On the digital front , the Quad introduced the " Quad Principles for Development and Deployment of Digital Public Infrastructure . " This set of principles focuses on equitable access , improved public service delivery , and fostering innovation and competition . India 's leadership in digital transformation is evident , as the country will offer technical assistance to interested Indo-Pacific nations , ensuring they can leverage DPI to enhance public services and drive innovation . <h> Reforming Global Governance : UN Security Council Expansion <p> A significant diplomatic achievement at the summit was the collective agreement to push for reforming the UN Security Council . The leaders recognized the urgent need to make the Council more representative , inclusive , and democratic . This reform seeks to expand both permanent and non-permanent membership categories , ensuring that the Security Council better @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's Role in Expanding Education and Clean Energy <p> Beyond the Quad 's collective initiatives , India announced individual efforts to foster development in the Indo-Pacific . India will offer scholarships for students from the region to pursue engineering degrees at its government-funded technical institutes . This educational initiative will help strengthen people-to-people ties and build the next generation of engineers equipped to handle future challenges . <p> Additionally , India committed to investing $2 million in solar projects in small island nations like Fiji , Comoros , Madagascar , and Seychelles . This investment underscores India 's focus on promoting clean energy and combating climate change , aligning with the broader Quad goal of advancing sustainable development .

@@114626037 <p> More than a decade ago , I brought to his notice that calculations of land use in Goa indicate that without converting land under forests and agriculture , Goa would have only 45,000 hectares , or 450 sq km , of land left for all future development . Ex-Chief Minister Manohar Parrikar took some time to review my calculations and then agreed with me . Hereafter , all the elections in Goa could be fought over land-related issues . But this smallest state in India , with a total land area of 3,701 sqkm , presents a perplexing governance paradox . Despite its manageable size , it faces administrative inefficiencies , environmental degradation , and an inability to cope with natural disasters . The root of this problem lies in a fundamental mismatch between the state 's compact geography and its bloated governance apparatus . <p> As an ecological historian , I argue that the state 's governance structure far exceeds its spatial requirements yet fails to deliver effective , people-centered outcomes . Including 11 islands and rocky outcrops encroached by the government of Karnataka near Canacona , as shown in their revenue records , the total land @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ After excluding government forests , which cover 1,25,000 hectares , and agro-horticulture land , which covers 1,44,000 hectares , the land governed by our government becomes much smaller . You do n't need all government departments to govern forest areas and agricultural lands . After eliminating this area , we are left with the magic number 1,01,100 hectares , or for easier understanding , just 1,011 sqkm . Yet , this small area is managed by a Chief Minister , 11 cabinet ministers , and over 65,000 government employees . Comparatively , countries like Monaco ( 2 sqkm ) , San Marino ( 61 sqkm ) , and even Singapore ( 728 sqkm ) manage their territories far more efficiently with leaner administrative structures . Even larger districts in India , such as those managed by a single district collector , govern areas more expansive than Goa 's 1,011 sqkm . <p> Urban planning expert Shruti Rajagopalan notes , " Governments are not necessarily more efficient in smaller spaces ; in fact , complexity without a need for it leads to overlapping jurisdictions and a lack of accountability " ( @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ system , where a multitude of departments and bureaucratic layers overcomplicate what should be a relatively simple administrative task . The result is a state caught in a web of inefficiency and inaction , where the machinery of governance is overextended and underproductive . Natural disasters like floods , cyclones , and epidemics have long been a part of Goa 's history . The former capital , Old Goa , endured waves of disease outbreaks , and some areas in Salcete and Mormugao were periodically flooded . Yet , Goa 's historical governance systems , particularly the Comunidade structure , allowed local communities to manage their resources effectively . This system was based on generational knowledge of the land , ensuring that land use , water management , and disaster response were rooted in sustainability and resilience . <p> Political economist Elinor Ostrom , who studied local governance models , emphasised , " When local communities are involved in the management of natural resources , they tend to produce outcomes that are more sustainable and responsive to environmental changes " ( Ostrom , 2009 ) . Goa 's traditional governance @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ environmental shocks . However , the transition from a **25;511;TOOLONG system to a centralised , consultant-driven model after statehood dismantled this resilience . Today , decisions are outsourced to expensive external consultants who lack an intimate understanding of Goa 's landscape , leading to development projects that degrade the environment and exacerbate disaster risks . The effects of this governance failure are most visible in Goa 's environmental degradation . Hills are being leveled for construction , rivers regularly flood , and landslides have become frequent . Roads sink , culverts collapse , and towns that historically never saw flooding face deluges . These symptoms point to a systemic failure of governance to enforce planning regulations or respect ecological limits . <p> Ecologist Madhav Gadgil 's research highlights that " the absence of micro-level spatial planning and the systematic weakening of traditional land-use systems have resulted in an erosion of Goa 's natural resilience " ( Gadgil , 2017 ) . In essence , the government has allowed unchecked development , particularly in vulnerable areas , without considering long-term environmental consequences . Goa 's governance model , designed for larger @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's unique spatial and environmental challenges . A 2020 report by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology warned that the state 's capacity to withstand future climate shocks is severely compromised due to poor land-use planning and governance failures . This is not just a failure of the administration but a looming environmental disaster that could have catastrophic consequences for Goa 's future . <p> Another critical factor contributing to Goa 's governance crisis is corruption . When governance is overburdened with bureaucracy , as in Goa , opportunities for corruption multiply . Transparency International 's 2022 report shows Goa ranks poorly in public sector transparency , with widespread reports of delays , bribes , and bureaucratic inefficiencies that hinder effective governance . Political scientist Samuel Paul observes that " corruption flourishes in environments where responsibility is diffused and where the chain of accountability is so long that it becomes difficult to pinpoint where failures occur " ( Paul , 2018 ) . In Goa , despite its small size , the complexity of governance ensures that no one is held accountable for failures in public services , environmental protection @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ governance issue is the absence of micro-level spatial planning , which accounts for local communities ' specific environmental , social , and economic needs . <p> Goa 's size makes it an ideal candidate for such localised , responsive planning . Yet , the current governance structure is centralised , disconnected from the ground realities , and largely driven by external consultants who lack contextual understanding . Urban planner Neha Sinha notes that " micro-level spatial planning , when implemented properly , allows for more tailored and responsive governance , reducing the risk of environmental degradation and improving the quality of life for residents " ( Sinha , 2021 ) . In Goa , returning to this governance model could solve many of the state 's problems . By integrating local knowledge with modern planning techniques , Goa could regain the resilience it once had . The solution to the state 's governance crisis is not more complexity but simplification . The state must streamline its governance structure , eliminate redundant departments , and focus on localised , community-driven decision-making . The current bloated system only maintains a status quo @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a unique opportunity . Goa 's future resilience depends on its ability to adapt to this principle . Its governance structure must be realigned to reflect its spatial scale . The state 's small size should allow for more efficient , responsive governance , but only if we simplify the system and empower local communities . The signalling is global goods , the translation is broadening the canvass of engagement . <p> It is clever crafting for sure - how else do you bring on board partners like India , which is reluctant to be a party to any military alliance . The framing is pertinent because it not only opens up space for bilateral security partnerships ( for instance the 2+2 format for India ) , but also for cross-cutting engagement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations ( ASEAN ) and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <h> What do we read for India ? <p> The key point of emphasis for India has been engagement without entanglements . Scholars on foreign policy and grand strategy would broadly define entanglements as the pressure that a country feels to engage in a conflict because of an alliance . <p> The entanglement trap is rooted in an era of Cold War politics marked by bi-polarity and military alliances . However , both historically and in moments of critical geopolitical churning , India has refrained from the entanglement trap in its own national interests and , of course , to guard its own strategic autonomy . <p> For a rising power like India , the Wilmington script has two-fold implications : First , it provides India the wherewithal to buttress its claim as a moral power with the material capability to deliver . So the commitment to the Quad Cancer Moonshot Initiative and a grant of HPV sampling kits , detection kits and cervical cancer vaccines worth $7.5 million to the Indo-Pacific region needs to be read in the context of strengthening the mechanism for global cooperation on health @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in its own national interests and , of course , to guard its own strategic autonomy . <p> And so should the other key announcements like a new category of scholarships for students of the Indo-Pacific region ( specifically for bachelors-level engineering programmes ) or the commitment for the development and deployment of Digital Public Infrastructure . <p> Secondly , without the formal architecture of a military alliance and with China 's increasing footprints in the Indo-Pacific , India has also very strategically aligned with Quad initiatives like the Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer Mission and the Maritime Initiative for Training in the Indo-Pacific ( MAITRI ) 2025 . <p> The common thread that runs through all this is the widening canvass of engagement , leveraging its interest vis-a-vis China , and more importantly , shaping the discourse on global governance and cooperation . <p> However , while the script sounds strategically pertinent , how this manifests in terms of bilateral engagements and beyond the Indo-Pacific needs to be seen , specifically given that India straddles both Russia and the US in the wake of the critical geopolitical churning . <h> Slippery @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ end of the spectrum , there is a growing strategic partnership with the US on the other . From India 's standpoint , its need and push for collaborative engagement in critical and emerging technologies , defence and strategic partnerships , and reform of the United Nations Security Council are all on a positive spin . <p> For the US , while it sees India as a potential bridge-builder in the conflict in Ukraine , or an important alliance partner to counterbalance China , it knows that it is difficult to nudge India away from its script of strategic autonomy . There is also no denying the fact that the US and India have definitely elevated their engagement to the level of deepened strategic partnership bilaterally . <p> So , what does India need to be watchful of ? First , double talk on the engagement on foreign policy and the slippery terrain of domestic politics . Foreign policymaking and grand strategy in the US are more complicated , which means India needs to pay greater attention to the differing voices in the US foreign policy establishment itself . It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on the Pannun case summons . <p> Second , given statecraft and great power politics , India needs to watch how the US navigates India 's interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean Rim Association region . While China is converging its interests , will the US still want an India with unfettered moral and material capabilities ? <p> So , of course , one needs to be watchful of the US in India 's neighbourhood as great powers are never weary of covert/overt ways of power maximisation . <p> Shweta Singh is associate professor , Department of International Relations , South Asian University .

@@114748055 <h> Study published last week looks at data from 1990 to 2021 to assess stroke cases in 204 countries . High ambient temperature saw 2nd-highest increase in any risk factor during the period . <p> New Delhi : Air pollution and high temperatures are some of the leading causes for stroke incidence and prevalence worldwide . A new report published online last week in the journal The Lancet Neurology looks at data from 1990 to 2021 to assess the occurrence , causes , risk factors and regional variations of stroke deaths across 204 countries . <p> The study is an analysis of the latest Global Burden of Disease ( GBD ) Study , published in 2021 . Led by neurologist Valery L Feigin , director of the Auckland University of Technology in New Zealand , it will appear in volume 23 , issue 10 of the journal in October . <p> South Asia , along with Latin America , Central Asia , and Africa , is one of the top regions where ambient air pollution is a high-risk factor for stroke-related deaths and disabilities . <p> Similarly , stroke-related deaths and disabilities attributed to other risk factors such as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ higher presence in South Asia as opposed to Western Europe or North America . Through these analyses , the study describes how strokes and their related causes differ across regions . <p> One of the most important trends noticed by this analysis is that after high systolic blood pressure , ambient air pollution was the second-highest risk factor for stroke-related deaths and disabilities worldwide . @@114748734 <h> Explained : How Climate Models Help Predict The Warming Of The Earth <h> Climate models can not predict everything because of the inherent chaos in the system but they are a tool to understand what might happen . <p> Vijaywada : A 2023 report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) , theUnited Nations body for assessing the science related to climate change , warned that global warming will likely exceed the limit of1.5 ? Cbefore the end of the century , against what countries had agreed at the 21st Conference of Parties in Paris ( COP ) in 2015 . This increase in temperature will lead to more frequent and intenseclimate-related risks like heat waves and floods . <p> " Projections about the future climate can help policy makers prepare for disasters , " says Professor S. Ravichandran from the Climate Studies program at the Indian Institute of Technology in Mumbai . <p> Projections about the future climate are made through climate models , which aid our understanding of how the climate had changed in the past and how it is evolving . These climate models are critical for India , a country heavily @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about climate , which is defined by " the long-term pattern of temperature and precipitation averages and extremes at a location , " and not about weather , which are the everyday changes in temperature , precipitation and so on , explains Ravichandran . Ravichandran studies fluidity , of gases or liquids , such as wind , on high-performing computers -- an important part of climate models . <p> " Climate models have predicted the warming of the planet as a result of anthropogenic CO2 emissions , the resulting rise of the mean sea level , the selective warming of the Arctic , the intensification of wet and dry extremes , etc. , " says Ravichandran . <p> Edited excerpts from an interview with Ravichandran , on what climate models are , how they work and their limitations , and what they mean for our lives . <p> What is a climate model ? <p> A global climate model is an approximate digital twin of the planet . It is digital in the sense that it lies inside a computer , and approximate because several processes in the real world @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the computer . The primary function of climate models is to test how the planet might react to external changes , or " forcing " . For instance , if we double the CO2 level in the atmosphere , what would happen to the temperature on the planet ? <p> How do climate models work ? <p> Global climate models ( GCMs ) have interacting components that model the behaviour of the atmosphere , the oceans , the land , the sea ice and life . These components individually model the parts of the earth system , and their interaction models the earth system as a whole . Any given forcing stress to the system such as more CO2 added to the system will affect all these component systems as well as their interactions , and GCMs predict the results . They do this by solving the governing equations ( basically , conservation laws for mass , momentum and energy ) in one , two or three spatial dimensions and time . <p> What are the different types of climate models and how do they work ? <p> Depending on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , there are several kinds of climate models . The simplest of these only deal with energy balance in one dimension : energy comes in from the sun radiatively , and the earth reflects some , and absorbs and re-radiates the rest . <p> The most complicated models include the effects of dozens of interacting processes in three dimensions . For example the rate at which plants and trees reflect or absorb radiation , release water vapour , absorb CO2 , etc would have been assumed in simpler climate models but are modelled in more recent , more sophisticated climate models . <p> What are the challenges in simulating climate at global and regional levels ? <p> Given a big enough computer , all the processes that make up the earth system can be computed . But such a computer would have to be very big indeed . The size of the computer required grows with the size of the system to be computed ; after all , the simplest " computer " that simulates the entire earth system is the earth itself . So the fundamental challenge of global @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ are essential and ignore the rest . This is easier said than done , and is an area of active ongoing research . <p> Global climate models can predict averages well . For instance , if human beings continue to dump CO2 into the atmosphere , the average surface temperature will increase . But this does not itself tell us what happens day-to-day in , for instance , Mumbai . This is the domain of regional climate modelling . <p> Regional climate models are typically run using inputs from the global climate models , and run on scales much smaller ( 1,000 km , as opposed to 40,000 km ) and over much shorter time horizons ( months to years , not decades ) . The resolution is orders of magnitude better than in global climate models and , depending on the model , more processes are modelled explicitly . The increased resolution requires a lot of computational resources . <p> Perhaps most importantly , both regional and global models are limited due to the internal variability of the Earth 's climate system . Internal variability is the naturally occurring @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It is made up of components that are predictable , such as the El Ni ? o -- Southern Oscillation warming of parts of the central Pacific , and unpredictable events because of the chaotic nature of the system . <p> In other words , the climate system is inherently chaotic and noisy , and rare events occur naturally . Attributing these events to climate change is a statistical exercise . <p> How do climate modellers overcome these challenges ? <p> Studies of processes--physical , chemical , biological--that affect the climate help improve climate models . Internal variability can be quantified and taken into account by performing ensemble simulations -- many simulations of the same events with small changes in the initial conditions or parameters . Improving the resolution of the climate models can also give better results . <p> However , both ensemble simulations and higher resolution simulations are computationally expensive , and faster climate models that can run on bigger computers are also an avenue of research . <p> What are the important things climate models have taught us so far ? <p> Climate models have predicted the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ emissions , the resulting rise of the mean sea level , the selective warming of the Arctic , the intensification of wet and dry extremes , etc . <p> How can climate models help us plan for changes in policy making ? <p> Projections about the future climate can help policy makers prepare for disasters . Climate projections can be used to generate hazard and risk maps for vulnerable regions . For instance , knowing that wet and dry extremes will occur more frequently , cities can invest in water harvesting and flood prevention . States and countries can also plan for the internal migration that will occur as people move to avoid climate impacts . <p> Projections on the annual and seasonal timescales are even more impactful . Regional climate predictions on the seasonal-to-subseasonal scales--consisting of the aforementioned risk and vulnerability maps , seasonal forecasts and timely early warnings for extreme events--can empower governments and local agencies to take action saving lives and preventing economic losses ( this is called the Ready-Set-Go framework ) . <p> We welcome feedback . Please write to respond@indiaspend.org . We reserve the right @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @

@@114748825 <p> Temperatures around 40 degrees celsius in the last week of September are not usual in Assam . Yet , with an adversely changing climate , people in the northeastern state are reporting health complications arising out of the ' heat dome effect ' for the past few days . <p> The heat dome effect is explained as a type of high-pressure system ( also known as anti-cyclone ) that forms over a large area in the atmosphere , and causes extremely hot and dry weather conditions . <p> So far , seven people in Assam have lost their lives due to the ongoing 40-degrees heat which the mobile phone applications flag as ' feels like 50 degrees ' . <p> What has exacerbated the crisis for the residents of Assam is that the unusually high temperatures are n't cooling down at night . <h> Host of factors <p> The weakening monsoon circulation , poor soil moisture , heavy exposure to sunlight , local factors like heavy deforestation and expanding industrial activity have all contributed towards the heat dome effect now prevalent over a week in Assam , according to experts . <p> " Usually , air circulation over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ emerging from the Bay of Bengal hits the region with low velocity winds that provide the much-needed moisture , causing short spells of showers throughout the month of September , " Rahul Mahanta , an associate professor specialising in climate science at Guwahati-based Cotton University , told Down To Earth ( DTE ) . <p> " This year , we noticed that the circulation is completely absent and in its place , a high-pressure system prevails over Assam and adjoining states . Another crucial factor in the region has been soil moisture which generally has a cooling effect during the night . However , this year , we have witnessed an absence of soil moisture as well which has led to the high night-time temperatures . Based on these observations on the air circulation above the region , one can see the presence of a heat-dome effect , " Mahanta elaborated . <p> The absence of the monsoonal circulation , according to Mahanta , can be attributed to the imminent collapse of the gulf stream , one of the jet streams that controls atmospheric circulation in the tropical areas . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ currently happening to air currents , which are largely threatened by climate change , " added Mahanta . <p> Besides these , the professor explained that external local factors like deforestation across the region , rapid industrialisation in the region and urban heat islands have significantly contributed to the heat .
